planting.note: Plant container-grown divisions in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; this is a running bamboo, so install a deep rhizome barrier before planting unless space allows free spreading.

directions: Makino bamboo is a Taiwan-native timber species prized for producing a dense, upright grove faster than most other cold-tolerant running Phyllostachys, with slender green culms that thicken and lean gracefully as the grove matures. Its spring shoots are widely harvested for eating in its native range, and gardeners in warm-temperate climates grow it both for screening and light culm harvest. Because it spreads by rhizome, confine it with a buried barrier or an isolated planting site such as an island bed unless a naturalized grove is the goal. It establishes quickly once the rhizome system is settled, so plan containment before the first full growing season rather than after.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in average to fertile, well-drained soil in full sun for the brightest color; this dwarf runner spreads by shallow rhizome and is easily contained with a lawn edger, mowing strip, or buried barrier.

directions: This small-statured bamboo produces broad leaves striped bright gold over green, with the variegation intensifying in full sun and fading toward solid green in heavy shade. It stays low and dense enough to serve as a running groundcover under trees, along a border edge, or spilling over a wall, and unlike taller running bamboos its shallow, modest rhizome spread is manageable without an elaborate barrier system. Cut the whole planting back hard to the ground in late winter each year; fresh new culms emerge with the cleanest, brightest striping, since old canes lose color and look tattered by season's end. It tolerates a range of soils but colors and fills in best with regular moisture and an annual spring feeding.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; it spreads by rhizome more slowly than most running bamboos but still benefits from a barrier or contained bed in mild climates.

directions: Koi bamboo is a curiosity-cultivar of arrow bamboo selected for lower culms that swell into knuckle-like bulges between the nodes, an oddity that collectors display as a container specimen or conversation-piece accent near a patio. The swelling is most pronounced on younger, vigorously growing culms and becomes less obvious as canes age, so periodically removing older culms keeps the novelty texture on display. It tolerates deep shade better than most bamboos and holds up well in a large container, where its more restrained spread is easy to manage. Divide congested clumps every few years to maintain vigorous new growth and the best expression of the swollen internodes.

planting.note: Set out container divisions in spring once soil has warmed, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; as a true clumping bamboo it needs no containment barrier, but give it ample open ground for its wide mature clump.

directions: Blue timber bamboo produces tall, straight culms coated in a powdery, chalky-blue wax when young, an unusual color among timber bamboos that gradually fades to green-gray as canes age and weather. The clump grows into an impressive vertical screen quickly in warm climates, with mature culms strong enough for light garden construction and craft use. Because it forms a true tight clump rather than spreading by long rhizomes, it works well as a large-scale privacy screen near property lines without the containment concerns of running species. Protect young plants from hard freezes for the first two winters; established clumps in warm zones recover well from occasional cold damage to the foliage.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in humus-rich, moisture-retentive soil in partial shade; this is a running bamboo, so contain it with a buried barrier or an isolated bed except where a naturalized cold-climate grove is wanted.

directions: Kuril bamboo is native to the cold forest understories of Hokkaido, Sakhalin, and the Kuril Islands and is among the most winter-hardy bamboos in cultivation, tolerating conditions far colder than nearly any Phyllostachys or Fargesia. Its broad, glossy leaves and dense rhizome mat make it an effective groundcover under deciduous trees where a running bamboo can be allowed room to spread. Snow cover in its native range protects the foliage through harsh winters, so in cultivation a light winter mulch helps where reliable snow cover is absent. It spreads steadily by rhizome and is best sited where that vigor is welcome, or contained with a barrier in smaller gardens.
